whatItIs.text: A small, shiny, dense-fleshed variety of the common bean, central to Latin American cooking; the dark seed coats are rich in anthocyanins.

historyNote.text: Black turtle beans are native to the Americas and only became widely grown in the United States after the Mexican-American War (1846-48); they anchor dishes from Brazilian feijoada to Cuban Moros y Cristianos.

howToChoose.text: From a can, look for intact beans in an undented can; from the dry shelf, expect uniform, glossy beans with few splits.

storage.text: Move opened canned beans to a covered container in the fridge; dry beans keep in an airtight jar in a cool cupboard. The rulebook has the timing.
storage.note: opened-can and cooked-bean windows live in the food-safety rulebook

useItUp.text: Stir soft beans into soup, mash into dips, or crisp them in a hot pan with cumin for taco filling.

substitutions.note: similar earthy depth, larger and less dense
creamier and milder; turns stews paler
